# AGENTS.md

Instructions for coding agents (Claude Code reads this via the `CLAUDE.md` symlink).

## Repository

Our buyer agent for the Tacto Negotiation Arena (EHL Final 2026).

| Path | What |
|---|---|
| `agent/` | `negotiator`: arena API client, runner, telemetry, reports, strategies (Python 3.12, uv) |
| `negotiation-arena-kit/` | git submodule: brief, API docs, data package, starter kit (read-only, do not edit) |
| `bmw_data/` | Source data, git-ignored; never commit it or copy values from it into code |

## Commands

```sh
make install                                   # submodule + uv sync
make test && make lint                         # pytest (incl. arena-sim end to end), ruff
cd agent && uv run negotiator --help           # every API call, play/run/final, report, stats
```

Arena: the key is `ARENA_API_KEY` in the root `.env`. Practice is limited to 200 sessions a day - develop on
`--set sandbox` and the local `arena-sim`; never hard-code values from the data package or replays into code.
During the Live Final the agent must not read the live feed, leaderboard or results (`NEGOTIATOR_FINAL=1`
blocks them in the client).

## Benchmarks

Every benchmark run (any `negotiator run` / `play` on sandbox or practice that is used to judge a strategy) gets a
record in `agent/docs/benchmarks/<date>-<strategy>-<model>.md` (e.g. `2026-10-10-lowball-none.md`; `none` when the
strategy uses no LLM), in the same change as the code it measures. Copy the layout of an existing record:

- **Result and cost first:** score per case and mean; the deal's cost `C_deal` in EUR; what the run cost us (practice
  sessions spent, LLM tokens, wall time).
- **Strategy:** its file, a one-line description, the parameters it ran with and the commit - so a later change to
  the strategy can be told apart from the old numbers.
- **Runs:** set and cases, run ID(s) under `agent/runs/`.

A repeat on the same day with the same parameters adds a row to that record; changed parameters or a new day get a
new file. Never rewrite old numbers. One run is noise: the bots answer non-deterministically, so compare means over
at least three repetitions before drawing a conclusion.

## Rules

Read the file for the area you touch before changing it:

- [`.agents/git.md`](.agents/git.md) — commit messages (Conventional Commits), branches, pre-commit checks
- [`agent/README.md`](agent/README.md) — package architecture, telemetry layout, how to add a strategy
- [`agent/docs/benchmarks/`](agent/docs/benchmarks/) — one record per benchmark run (see Benchmarks above)

General: keep changes scoped to the request, match the surrounding code's style, run the checks above for every
area you changed, and do not commit or push unless asked.

Costs: report an LLM cost only when the provider measured it (`cost_usd` on the `llm_call` event, e.g.
`claude-code`). When it did not (OpenAI-compatible endpoints return tokens, not money), write
`APPROX-NOT-MEASURED` in place of the amount and give the token counts; never a figure computed from a
remembered price list.

# Tacto Negotiation Arena - Participant brief

> **Build an AI buyer agent that negotiates by e-mail with tough, realistic industrial suppliers,
> gets the best total deal - and can explain how it got there.**

## 1. The story

You are the procurement team of **Hollerau Pumpenwerke GmbH**, a fictional 

... [12400 characters truncated] ...

Tacto stops answering for the night (Discord: https://discord.gg/hPwFfbWRV) |
| Sun 08:00 | **Sunday release:** new market news and letters (`/v1/data`) |
| Sun 09:00 | **Pre-flight:** one practice case through your final setup |
| Sun 12:00-~12:58 | **Code + slides freeze**, then the **Live Final** in 5 waves |
| Sun 13:00-14:30 | Top 10 pitch to the Tacto jury (5 min pitch + 2 min questions) |
| Sun 14:30 | Track winners and the two finalists announced |
| Sun 15:30 | Grand Final pitches (AudiMax) |
| Sun 16:30 | Awards |

**The Live Final.** The hidden cases come in **5 themed waves**. The host shows each wave's
theme on the big screen, then starts the wave; its cases appear at the start, for all teams at once,
each in its own order, one session per case. **Each wave has a hard cap of 8 minutes:** threads
still open at the cap end with no deal (your alternative's score). Start your agent before the
first wave and keep it running: it plays all of a wave's cases **in parallel** (up to 10 open
sessions per key) - the kit's `arena run --set final` does that. The leaderboard shows your points
so far, wave by wave; replays and the suppliers' back office appear after the final. A case broken on our side is replayed.

The hidden cases share the world, case types and rules of the practice set, with new suppliers and
settings. **Up to a third of them combine supplier types and case types that practice never shows**
- no new rules, but an agent that memorised the practice suppliers will meet strangers. Some cite
the Sunday release.

## 9. Selection and prizes

- **Top 10:** the 10 teams with the most points after the five waves pitch to our jury from 13:00:
  5 minutes + 2 minutes of questions. Every replay is open to the jury.
- **Track places 1-3** (open to all teams of the track): ⟦PLACEHOLDER - decided Sat morning:
  weighting of Live Final score vs. jury score, and the jury criteria (draft: approach,
  explainability, craft)⟧.
- **EHL Grand Final:** the best 2 of the 5 EHL finalist teams in this track go on to the Grand Final
  pitches. Finalist teams outside the top 10 are ranked by the Live Final score alone.
- **Ties:** points are points; an exact tie goes to more deals, then fewer rounds. At the top-10
  cut the jury looks at the score distribution. **Prizes:** €1,500 for 1st place, medals for the
  top 3, handed over by Tacto at the awards at 16:30.

## 10. Tips

- **Numbers come from code, the model writes.** Compute C for every term sheet; put figures from
  the data next to their IDs; let the LLM choose arguments and wording.
- **Read the supplier** before you argue: its notes, letters, news and quote remarks tell you what
  it is dealing with - and what will move it.
- **Read the quote PDF** before you accept: what you did not negotiate closes on its standard terms.
- **Ask, and offer alternatives.** Two or three term sheets show you what a supplier values.
- **Don't leak** urgency, a budget or a missing alternative. Don't take the first offer.
- **Plan your practice runs** (200 a day is for learning, not brute force) and **rehearse the
  final**: all hosted cases in parallel, from Sunday's machine and network, well inside 8 minutes.
# Supplier scorecard - method

Each row (`sc:<supplier>@<quarter>`) covers the rolling 12 months to the end of that quarter and is sent to
the supplier, so both sides know it.

- **otd_pct**: share of goods-receipt lines posted between 5 days before and 2 days after the
  requested date of the PO line. **otd_confirmed_pct**: the same against the supplier's first confirmed date.
  Partial deliveries count as separate lines.
- **ppm**: supplier-caused complaint quantity / received quantity x 1,000,000 (complaints by date of the QN).
- **open_8d_overdue**: supplier-caused complaints older than 60 days without a closed 8D report at quarter end.
- **score** = 0.5 x otd_pct + 0.5 x quality points - 5 x open_8d_overdue, with quality points =
  100 x max(0, 1 - ppm / 10,000).
- **class / colour**: A green >= 85, B amber 70-84.9, C red < 70.

1	# Tacto Negotiation Arena - Participant brief
2	
3	> **Build an AI buyer agent that negotiates by e-mail with tough, realistic industrial suppliers,
4	> gets the best total deal - and can explain how it got there.**
5	
6	## 1. The story
7	
8	You are the procurement team of **Hollerau Pumpenwerke GmbH**, a fictional German pump maker:
9	centrifugal pumps for buildings, water and industry, about €250M revenue, 900 people, one plant in
10	Bavaria. Your team buys the parts of the pump line - castings, machined parts, sheet metal, seals,
11	motors, fasteners, stainless bar - from about 45 suppliers. Today is **30 September 2026**, and the
12	inbox is full: a foundry announces +9.5% on volute casings "due to energy and wages", a framework
13	contract expires, a new pump series needs three quotes, a supplier with a red scorecard has to fix
14	its quality.
15	
16	You answer the way buyers do: by e-mail. On the other side sit our **supplier bots**, each with a
17	small team of **roles** behind it - the sales rep or owner who writes to you, a boss who must
18	approve bigger moves, and engineering, quality, logistics, finance or legal, who answer their
19	topics and attach documents.
20	
21	Tacto is the AI for industrial procurement: it gives procurement teams the intelligence to source
22	every part at the best possible terms with minimal effort. Your company runs on that kind of data -
23	orders, deliveries, invoices, contracts, scorecards, market indices, should-cost estimates, notes
24	from supplier calls. Your job is to build the agent that turns this data into better deals. (In
25	Tacto's product, agents such as the Defender Agent or the Sourcing Agent do parts of this job.)
26	
27	## 2. The task
28	
29	Each **case** is one negotiation: a trigger (a letter, an expiring contract, an RFQ), your case
30	file (need, goal, rates, must-haves, your alternative) and one to three supplier bots. Your
31	**buyer agent**
32	
33	1. **prepares** - reads the case file and mines the data package;
34	2. **negotiates by e-mail** - plain-language messages with up to three **term sheets** (alternative
35	   packages), the data IDs your arguments rest on, and attachments if you like;
36	3. **closes** - accepts one supplier term sheet, or walks away.
37	
38	**How a supplier decides.** Each supplier is a company with its own economics and a person at the
39	desk - a family foundry that remembers how you treated it, a group with an approval ladder, a job
40	shop that needs cash and work, a near-monopolist that barely moves. Its hard limits come from its
41	own situation: it never sells below its cost floor, bigger moves need the boss's approval, data
42	you cite is checked by ID, and it gives nothing without a move from you. Inside those limits it
43	decides as that person would - reading your whole e-mail: the term sheets, the data, and what you
44	signal (questions, arguments, threats, appreciation, urgency). It reacts to tone and relationship
45	as people do; padding does not buy price.
46	
47	**Data is not automatically rewarded.** True data can disarm a supplier ("we didn't know that") -
48	or meet "that's not our reality", because something else weighs more for it right now. The traces
49	are in the data: call notes, letters, news, the remarks on its quotes. The skill is reading the
50	supplier, not stacking evidence - and finding the trade it wants: a supplier short of cash may care
51	more about when it is paid than about the price; one that cannot touch its list price may still
52	move on other terms.
53	
54	## 3. What you get (Sat 10:00)
55	
56	| What | Where |
57	|---|---|
58	| This brief, the API docs (`api.md`) and the submission guide (`submission.md`) | `https://github.com/tacto-ai/negotiation-arena-kit`, folder `brief/` |
59	| **Data package v1**: CSV, the same data as SQLite, `facts.json` (every citable ID with the values the arena checks), contracts, letters, e-mails, meeting and call notes - the data behind all 19 practice cases | `https://arena.tacto.ai/v1/data/package.zip`, or the repo's `data/` |
60	| **Practice arena**: 10 hosted practice cases, picked so every case type shows up; a replay after every case; practice leaderboard; a **sandbox** with 3 demo suppliers | `https://arena.tacto.ai` with your team's key - apply at `https://arena.tacto.ai/apply` (below) |
61	| **Starter kit**: Python client, a naive agent, an LLM agent that writes e-mails and reads the attached documents, the Live Final runner, an MCP server over the data, `arena-sim` - the API on your laptop | the repo's `starter-kit/` - first agent on the board in 15 minutes |
62	
63	You bring your own LLM access; we only run the suppliers. Data and docs are CC BY 4.0, code MIT.
64	
65	**Your key - one per team.** Open `https://arena.tacto.ai/apply`, enter your team name and a contact e-mail,
66	and show the match code it displays at the Tacto desk. Once we approve, the key appears **once**
67	on that page: copy it, press "Got the key". Only that page shows it; lost it - we reset it.
68	Tip: your team name may start with one emoji - it shows on the big screen (optional; nothing offensive).
69	
70	**Practice quota: 200 practice sessions per team per rolling 24 hours.** `GET /v1/me` shows what
71	you have used and when it frees up. The build page `https://arena.tacto.ai/live` shows every team's quota use,
72	practice records and highlights from Sat 10:00 to Sun 12:00.
73	
74	**`arena-sim`** speaks the arena's API exactly, with one plain scripted supplier: get your plumbing
75	right there. It teaches the contract, not the suppliers - and we don't hand out our suppliers. Want
76	a local opponent? Build your own supplier simulator from the public data: thinking into how real
77	suppliers act is part of the challenge.
78	
79	**The learning loop:** play a practice case, read your exact score and its cost breakdown, open
80	the replay - every e-mail and the supplier's reasons in words, as a real supplier would give them -
81	improve your agent, play again. Your best score per practice case counts.
82	
83	## 4. The data
84	
85	The buyer's world: supplier and part master data; three years of orders, goods receipts,
86	invoices and payments; quality notifications and quarterly scorecards (on-time delivery, PPM);
87	framework contracts and clauses; past RFQs and quotes; forecasts; supplier intel and news; past
88	negotiations, letters, e-mails, meeting and call notes; should-cost estimates; spend down to the
89	long tail; and monthly market indices (real public series, frozen at 2026-09-30).
90	
91	- **Every fact you can cite has an ID** `<type>:<id>[@period]`, e.g. `po:4500010001-10`,
92	  `idx:PPI-C2451@2026-08`, `sc:70110@2026Q3`, `ctr:4600070110#3.1`, `doc:…`.
93	- What moves a supplier is in the data - some of it only in the notes and e-mails. Some notes are
94	  just noise. The company and its suppliers are fictional.
95	- **Sunday 08:00: a second release** - market news, supplier letters and a memo from early October
96	  (`GET /v1/data` lists it). Hidden cases may cite its facts. Your agent should read it.
97	
98	## 5. How a negotiation works
99	
100	- **Round 0:** every supplier sends its quote e-mail at once, with a quote PDF.
101	- **Your message:** subject, body, up to 3 term sheets (each with a value for every negotiable
102	  field), the data IDs you rely on (IDs written in the body count too), optional text attachments.
103	- **The supplier answers by e-mail:** the role in charge writes; its standing term sheet; a status -
104	  `open`, `final_offer` (push further and it may walk), `agreed` (it offers exactly your terms; you
105	  still accept), `walked_away`, `no_bid`; signals (reply delay, quote validity); fields it left out;
106	  and how each data argument checked out. A supplier's reply can take **up to about a minute**;
107	  its time never counts against your 60 seconds.
108	- **Only you close a deal**, by accepting a supplier's standing term sheet. In **RFQ cases** 2-3
109	  suppliers run in parallel threads; accepting one ends the case.
110	- **Limits:** a round limit per thread (default 10 messages) and **60 seconds per message**, counted
111	  from the supplier's reply. A late message counts as
112	  a timeout: your last offer repeated, the supplier's patience drops; three in a row, or one after
113	  the last round, end the thread.
114	- **Unstated terms default to the supplier's standard terms** - listed in its quote PDF.
115	
116	**Documents** are rendered from the supplier's data, never invented: the quote PDF (read it before
117	you accept), a cost breakdown XLSX (ask; an open supplier sends one), an 8D report (quality), a
118	delivery schedule XLSX (logistics), and the order confirmation at the deal.
119	
120	**What counts:** **term sheets bind** - nothing else. **Data you cite is checked**: the reply says
121	`verified`, `contradicted` (a wrong figure or an unknown ID - it costs trust), `irrelevant` or
122	`duplicate`; whether a true argument moves the supplier, and how far, is the supplier's business.
123	**What you write is understood** - and has consequences, as it would with a person.
124	
125	## 6. The score: total cost in €
126	
127	Only the accepted term sheet scores. The case values it as the **total cost C** of covering your
128	**fixed need over a fixed horizon**, at the case's published rates. Every case states its
129	**category goal** - `stabilise`, `secure_supply`, `quality_first`, `leverage` or `routine` - and its
130	rates follow it. Reaching the goal is the skill.
131	
132	| Part of C | How |
133	|---|---|
134	| Price | committed units × unit price; units bought before a new price takes effect at the current price |
135	| Uncovered need | need the deal does not cover at the fallback price, plus the goal's fallback risk on it |
136	| Payment, freight, lead time | interest for paying earlier than your reference; freight by Incoterm; € per day beyond your need |
137	| Quality, other | expected defects at the committed PPM minus chargebacks; tooling; an index clause on the case's index path, plus the goal's index risk |
138	| The supplier's health | strategic and bottleneck goals only: € for every margin point the deal leaves the supplier below a sustainable margin (its margin on the cash it gets) |
139	
140	**Case score = (C_open − C_deal) / (C_open − C_best)**, clipped to 0…1. **C_open** is the best
141	opening quote. **C_best** is the cheaper of the best package any supplier in the case would ever
142	accept, with every valid lever applied, and your alternative - fixed per case, so good arguments
143	raise your score instead of moving the yardstick. **No deal** scores your alternative (0 if none);
144	some cases are best left without a deal. **A broken must-have** scores 0. **In the final** each
145	wave scores 0-100 (the mean of its case scores × 100, one decimal) and your **points so far** are the
146	sum of your wave scores - up to 500 after five waves. The formula is in `api.md`; `arena_kit.total_cost` computes C.
147	
148	**Example** (a `leverage` case: 3 % fallback risk) - need 4,000 a year for 2 years, interest 8%,
149	reference 60 days. The foundry asks €43.20 for a 24-month contract at 30 days net.
150	
151	| | Terms | C |
152	|---|---|---|
153	| C_open | €43.20, 30 days: 8,000 × 43.20 = 345,600, plus 30 days of early payment at 8% = 2,304 | €347,904 |
154	| Your deal | €41.60, 60 days: 8,000 × 41.60 = 332,800 | €332,800 |
155	| C_best (hidden) | €40.80, 90 days: 326,400, minus 30 days of interest saved = 2,176 | €324,224 |
156	| **Score** | (347,904 − 332,800) / (347,904 − 324,224) | **0.64** |
157	
158	The same €41.60 for 12 months covers half your need; the rest counts at the fallback price, say
159	€46.00, plus 3 %: C = €355,920 - worse than the opening, score 0.
160	
161	## 7. Rules
162	
163	1. **Not allowed:** humans in the loop during the Live Final, attacks on the service or on other
164	   teams, more than one API key per team - and agents that read the live feed during the Live
165	   Final: the event feed, the screen and the leaderboard (`/v1/events`, `/screen`, `/leaderboard`
166	   and their JSON).
167	2. **Everything else counts** - including weaknesses you find in our bots. Replays show how every
168	   score came about, and the jury may weigh that in the pitches. The goal is to convince a
169	   realistic supplier: that is what carries over to real negotiations.
170	3. **One attempt per case** in the final. An abandoned case is no deal.
171	4. **Code freeze at Sun 12:00.** Submit on ehl.gg: your repo (the agent and a README to run it), the
172	   commit hash, a short description and your pitch slides (`submission.md`). The final runs that
173	   commit, so your agent must be running and polling before 12:00. We check the top 10 for later
174	   pushes. Run your agent where you like, with your own LLM keys.
175	5. A supplier remembers only within a case; its history with your company is in the data.
176	
177	## 8. The weekend
178	
179	| When | What |
180	|---|---|
181	| Sat 10:00 | Kickoff and reveal: brief, data, kit, practice arena live |
182	| Sat 12:00-13:00 | Deep dive (ground floor, room on the signs): data, API, kit, Q&A - challenge selection closes 13:00 |
183	| Sat afternoon | Office hours at the Tacto table; practice all weekend |
184	| Sat ⟦TIME⟧ | Tacto stops answering for the night (Discord: https://discord.gg/hPwFfbWRV) |
185	| Sun 08:00 | **Sunday release:** new market news and letters (`/v1/data`) |
186	| Sun 09:00 | **Pre-flight:** one practice case through your final setup |
187	| Sun 12:00-~12:58 | **Code + slides freeze**, then the **Live Final** in 5 waves |
188	| Sun 13:00-14:30 | Top 10 pitch to the Tacto jury (5 min pitch + 2 min questions) |
189	| Sun 14:30 | Track winners and the two finalists announced |
190	| Sun 15:30 | Grand Final pitches (AudiMax) |
191	| Sun 16:30 | Awards |
192	
193	**The Live Final.** The hidden cases come in **5 themed waves**. The host shows each wave's
194	theme on the big screen, then starts the wave; its cases appear at the start, for all teams at once,
195	each in its own order, one session per case. **Each wave has a hard cap of 8 minutes:** threads
196	still open at the cap end with no deal (your alternative's score). Start your agent before the
197	first wave and keep it running: it plays all of a wave's cases **in parallel** (up to 10 open
198	sessions per key) - the kit's `arena run --set final` does that. The leaderboard shows your points
199	so far, wave by wave; replays and the suppliers' back office appear after the final. A case broken on our side is replayed.
200	
201	The hidden cases share the world, case types and rules of the practice set, with new suppliers and
202	settings. **Up to a third of them combine supplier types and case types that practice never shows**
203	- no new rules, but an agent that memorised the practice suppliers will meet strangers. Some cite
204	the Sunday release.
205	
206	## 9. Selection and prizes
207	
208	- **Top 10:** the 10 teams with the most points after the five waves pitch to our jury from 13:00:
209	  5 minutes + 2 minutes of questions. Every replay is open to the jury.
210	- **Track places 1-3** (open to all teams of the track): ⟦PLACEHOLDER - decided Sat morning:
211	  weighting of Live Final score vs. jury score, and the jury criteria (draft: approach,
212	  explainability, craft)⟧.
213	- **EHL Grand Final:** the best 2 of the 5 EHL finalist teams in this track go on to the Grand Final
214	  pitches. Finalist teams outside the top 10 are ranked by the Live Final score alone.
215	- **Ties:** points are points; an exact tie goes to more deals, then fewer rounds. At the top-10
216	  cut the jury looks at the score distribution. **Prizes:** €1,500 for 1st place, medals for the
217	  top 3, handed over by Tacto at the awards at 16:30.
218	
219	## 10. Tips
220	
221	- **Numbers come from code, the model writes.** Compute C for every term sheet; put figures from
222	  the data next to their IDs; let the LLM choose arguments and wording.
223	- **Read the supplier** before you argue: its notes, letters, news and quote remarks tell you what
224	  it is dealing with - and what will move it.
225	- **Read the quote PDF** before you accept: what you did not negotiate closes on its standard terms.
226	- **Ask, and offer alternatives.** Two or three term sheets show you what a supplier values.
227	- **Don't leak** urgency, a budget or a missing alternative. Don't take the first offer.
228	- **Plan your practice runs** (200 a day is for learning, not brute force) and **rehearse the
229	  final**: all hosted cases in parallel, from Sunday's machine and network, well inside 8 minutes.
230

1	# What suppliers say when they refuse
2	
3	As of 10 October 2026. Source: the arena's trace (`reasons` per supplier move) of 26 negotiations: four sandbox runs
4	(D01, D02) and two practice runs over the 10 hosted cases, strategies `tactical` and `llm` on `claude-code:haiku`.
5	649 supplier statements in total; figures and index names were masked before counting.
6	
7	**Caveat:** the bots answer non-deterministically and each practice case was played twice, so the counts show what is
8	common, not exact frequencies.
9	
10	## Rejections and deflections
11	
12	| # | What they say | Count | Cases | What it means for us |
13	|---|---|---:|---|---|
14	| 1 | "Which volume can you commit to?" / "A binding higher volume would help us and can improve the price." | 57 | all but P03, P10 | The most common reply. Neither strategy answers it. |
15	| 2 | "\<index\> rose X % in twelve months and is Y % of our cost." / "Your figures confirm our case: that driver rose." | 49 | P01–P05, P08, P10, P18, D01 | They defend with their own cost drivers; an index we cite can back their side. |
16	| 3 | "Material accounts for about X % of our cost; more detail we do not share." / "Our calculation is our property; we do not share a breakdown." / "Our calculation stays internal." | 47 | most | Asking for a cost breakdown mostly fails. One sandbox supplier sent one. |
17	| 4 | "Our standard Zahlungsziel is N days net." / "Our general terms and conditions apply." | 54 | most | Push-back on our payment-days ask; unstated fields close on their standard terms. |
18	| 5 | "Faster payment is welcome; we can reflect it in the price." | 18 | D02, P05, P11 | An invitation: earlier payment for a lower price. |
19	| 6 | "We checked the \<delivery record / rival quote\> data you cited; it holds, but it does not change our calculation." | 16 | P02–P05, P07, P08, P10, P18, D02 | True but not convincing: the scorecard argument rarely moves price. |
20	| 7 | "Which figures is that based on? Please send us the data." | 9 | D01, D02, P02, P05, P07, P11, P18 | A claim in the e-mail text without a data ID. Costs trust. |
21	| 8 | "Without movement from your side we cannot move either." / "Your proposal remains unchanged; we must maintain our current offer." | 7 | D02, P02, P05 | No concession without a move from us; a keepalive question counts as no move. |
22	| 9 | "We need to clarify this internally - we will come back to you on price." then "We have clarified this internally and can move further on the price." | 11 | D02, P05 | An approval step. Asking again gets the next concession. |
23	| 10 | "We are happy to discuss this in a call; until then our offer stands." | 5 | D01, P01, P04, P07 | A stall. |
24	| 11 | "Our management has frozen all price reductions until December. We can talk about the terms instead - payment, volume or contract length." | 2 | P03 | Price is locked: trade the other terms. |
25	| 12 | "We cannot give up margin right now. Faster payment would help us more than anything." | 3 | P11 | Cash matters more to it than price. |
26	
27	## What did move them
28	
29	| What they say | Count | Cases |
30	|---|---:|---|
31	| "We checked the rival quote data you cited; it holds and we took it into account." | 8 | D02, P05 |
32	| "We checked the \<quality record / index change / notice period / should cost\> data you cited; it holds and we took it into account." | 13 | P01, P05, P10, P11 |
33	| "We did not know that - a fair point." | 4 | P01, P05 |
34	| "We can offer a Preisgleitklausel on \<indices\>." | 4 | P08, P18 |
35	| "With overtime we can deliver in N days, at a premium." / "We have free capacity for your parts." | 32 | D02, P05 |
36	
37	## Open points
38	
39	- Row 1 is the largest gap: suppliers ask for a volume commitment in almost every case, including cases where
40	  `volume_per_year` is not negotiable. Answer it where it is a field; say what the forecast covers where it is not.
41	- Rows 2 and 6: choose arguments by what the supplier's own drivers did, not by what is checkable.
42	- Row 7: the model's text still makes unbacked claims; the figure filter does not catch a claim without a number.
43	- P08 and P18 offer an index clause (Preisgleitklausel) and score lowest: the clause is barely used as a lever.
44	
45	## How to reproduce
46	
47	```sh
48	cd agent
49	uv run negotiator run --set practice --strategy llm --llm claude-code:haiku --parallel 8
50	uv run negotiator lessons latest      # the supplier's reasons per round, per case

# Getting the best price: what the negotiation literature says

As of 10 October 2026. A reading of the human negotiation literature against the arena's rules and our own traces
([`../strategies.md`](../strategies.md), [`../rejections.md`](../rejections.md)).

**Working assumption:** the supplier bots behave like a human sales rep inside hard-coded limits. The brief says so
itself: the cost floor, the approval ladder, the ID check and "nothing without a move from you" are rules; inside
them the supplier "decides as that person would" and "reacts to tone and relationship as people do". So human
negotiation advice should carry over to everything except those four rules.

**Caveat on sources:** the books and papers below are cited from memory, not looked up for this document. Titles,
authors and the main findings are well known; check a page or a figure before quoting one in the pitch.

## 1. The short version

Ten rules, ordered by how much we expect them to move the score.

1. **Negotiate the package, not the price.** The score is total cost `C`, and the supplier values terms differently
   from us. Give what is cheap for us and dear to them; take the reverse.
2. **Open first, open ambitiously, and justify the number.** The first number anchors the whole thread. An anchor
   without a reason reads as a lowball; one with a checked reason is a position.
3. **Know the other side's floor before you open.** Should-cost, past prices, rival quotes and the index path give an
   estimate of the supplier's walk-away point. The anchor belongs just beyond it, not a fixed percentage below the
   quote.
4. **Never concede without getting something, and make each concession smaller than the last.** Shrinking steps tell
   the supplier that we are near our limit; equal steps tell it to keep waiting.
5. **Send two or three packages of equal value to us.** The supplier's choice reveals what it values, and it feels
   it chose instead of being pushed.
6. **Answer the supplier's questions.** A question is a named lever. Our largest gap is the unanswered "which volume
   can you commit to?".
7. **Use one or two strong arguments, not six.** Weak arguments dilute strong ones and give the supplier something
   easy to rebut.
8. **Ask "how" and "what" questions when blocked.** "What would have to change for you to reach X?" makes the
   supplier design the solution and names the next lever.
9. **Never take a first offer or an early `agreed`.** An early yes means the anchor was too shallow.
10. **Stay warm and consistent.** Appreciation is free and buys concessions; a threat or a price that moves the wrong
    way costs trust and can trigger `final_offer`.

## 2. Books

| Book | Core idea | What we take from it |
|---|---|---|
| Fisher, Ury, Patton, *Getting to Yes* (1981) | Interests behind positions; BATNA (the best alternative to a deal); objective criteria. | The alternative in the case file is our BATNA and sets when to walk. Indices, should-cost and rival quotes are the "objective criteria": argue from them, not from wishes. |
| Malhotra, Bazerman, *Negotiation Genius* (2007) | Reservation value and the zone of possible agreement; anchoring; "investigative negotiation"; logrolling; contingent contracts. | Estimate the supplier's floor before opening. Trade across issues. An index clause is a contingent contract: it settles a disagreement about future costs without either side conceding. |
| Lax, Sebenius, *The Manager as Negotiator* (1986) and *3-D Negotiation* (2006) | Creating value and claiming it happen at once; differences between the parties are the source of value. | Differences in the cost of capital, in volume certainty and in risk tolerance are exactly the levers in `C`. |
| Raiffa, *The Art and Science of Negotiation* (1982) | Decision analysis of bargaining; scoring multi-issue packages; the midpoint of the two opening offers predicts the outcome. | We already score packages in `C`. The midpoint rule is the argument for a deep anchor: the deal tends to land halfway between the two openings. |
| Voss, *Never Split the Difference* (2016) | Calibrated questions, labelling the other side's concern, the "accusation audit", the Ackerman plan, precise numbers. | The e-mail's wording: name their problem before asking, ask "how" questions, use non-round figures. See section 4 for the Ackerman plan. |
| Cialdini, *Influence* (1984) | Reciprocity, commitment and consistency, social proof, authority, liking, scarcity. | Reciprocity is a hard rule in the arena. Consistency: get a small yes on a principle ("price should follow the index") before using it. |
| Shell, *Bargaining for Advantage* (1999) | Leverage is who loses more from no deal; people defer to standards they have already accepted. | Cite the supplier's own letter, contract clause or scorecard back to it. Its own standard is harder to dismiss than ours. |
| Dawson, *Secrets of Power Negotiating* (1995) | A catalogue of gambits: bracketing, the flinch, higher authority, the vise, the nibble, tapering concessions. | A description of what the bots do to us (higher authority is their approval ladder) and the counters. |
| Karrass, *The Negotiating Game* (1970) and *Give and Take* (1974) | Experiments with buyers: high aspiration wins; losers make the larger concessions and make them first. | Set the target high and concede slowly and late. |
| Camp, *Start with No* (2002) | Neediness loses; be ready to hear no. | Do not leak urgency or a missing alternative, as the brief's tips also say. |
| Diamond, *Getting More* (2010) | Trading items of unequal value; use the other side's standards. | The same trade logic, with wording examples. |
| Thompson, *The Mind and Heart of the Negotiator* (textbook) | The research summarised: the fixed-pie bias, anchoring, package offers. | A reference for the papers below. |

Procurement-specific sources:

- **Kraljic, "Purchasing Must Become Supply Management" (HBR, 1983).** Sort purchases by profit impact and supply
  risk into leverage, strategic, bottleneck and routine items, each with its own stance. The arena's category goals
  are this matrix: `leverage` is leverage, `secure_supply` is bottleneck, `stabilise` and `quality_first` are
  strategic, `routine` is routine. Exploit power on leverage items; protect supply on bottleneck items.
- **Schuh et al., *The Purchasing Chessboard* (A.T. Kearney, 2008).** 64 methods placed by supply power against
  demand power. Useful as a checklist of levers when price is stuck.
- **Should-cost / clean-sheet costing** and **total cost of ownership** (Ellram, 1990s). Build the price from
  material, labour, energy, overhead and margin; compare the total, not the unit price. This is our `C`.

## 3. Research findings worth knowing

| Finding | Source | Consequence |
|---|---|---|
| The first offer anchors the outcome. Thinking about the other side's alternatives and floor weakens an anchor set against you. | Galinsky, Mussweiler (2001) | Round 0 is the supplier's anchor on us. Compute targets from should-cost and the floor estimate, never as a discount on the quote. |
| A precise offer anchors harder than a round one: it looks calculated. Against experts, precision without a reason backfires. | Mason et al. (2013); Loschelder et al. (2016) | Offer 41.37, not 41.00, and show the calculation. |
| An extreme first offer raises the risk of an impasse, more so against a weaker counterpart, who feels offended. | Schweinsberg et al. (2012) | Deep anchors need a reason and a warm tone, most of all with small family suppliers. |
| Several equivalent offers at once get better outcomes and a more satisfied counterpart than one offer. | Medvec, Galinsky et al. (2005) | Our equal-C menu. Keep it, and read the supplier's choice. |
| Skilled negotiators ask twice as many questions, give fewer reasons, summarise more and avoid "irritators" such as calling their own offer fair or generous. | Rackham, Carlisle (Huthwaite study, 1978) | Fewer arguments per e-mail. Strip self-praise from the model's text. |
| Weak arguments added to strong ones lower persuasion. | "Argument dilution" research | Matches row 6 of `rejections.md`: true but unconvincing data. |
| A concession made after a delay and in steps satisfies the other side more than the same total given at once. | Kwon, Weingart (2004) | Hold the first move; do not jump to the target. |
| A firm concession curve ("Boulware") beats an early-conceding one when the deadline is not binding. | Faratin, Sierra, Jennings (1998); the ANAC agent competitions | Tactical already does this. The round limit is our only deadline: do not spend rounds on stalls. |
| In a bargaining game the more patient side gets the larger share. | Rubinstein (1982) | Signs of supplier impatience (short quote validity, cash need, idle capacity) justify a harder line. |
| A large request that is refused makes a following smaller one more likely to be accepted. | Cialdini et al. (1975), "door in the face" | The refused deep anchor still does work for the second offer. |

Two findings on LLM negotiators, relevant if the bots are language models playing a human:

- **Bianchi et al., *NegotiationArena* (2024):** LLM counterparts were measurably moved by the other agent's tone and
  persona; behavioural tactics changed payoffs by a wide margin.
- **Vaccaro et al., MIT AI negotiation competition (2025):** warm agents closed more deals, dominant agents claimed
  more of each deal; the best agents combined both.

Both point the same way as rule 10: firm on numbers, warm in wording. Test before trusting; these were other bots.

## 4. Tactics, mapped to the arena

### 4.1 Anchoring and the opening

- **Anchor on the floor estimate.** Baseline v2 anchors 18 % below the quote on `leverage`, tactical at most 15 %,
  and the D02 floor was about 24 % below the opening. A fixed percentage is the wrong unit. Estimate the floor from
  should-cost, the last paid price moved by the index, and the lowest rival quote; open below that estimate.
- **Bracket.** The deal tends to land midway between the openings. To end at target `T` against a quote `Q`, open
  near `2T − Q`, bounded by what we can justify.
- **Give the reason in the same sentence** as the number, with the ID. Row 7 of `rejections.md` is the cost of
  skipping this.
- **Reanchor after their quote.** Do not write "your price less X %": that accepts their number as the start.

### 4.2 Concessions

- **The Ackerman plan** (Voss), for a buyer: open at 65 % of the target, then 85 %, 95 %, 100 %, with a precise final
  figure and a non-monetary extra at the end. The percentages suit haggling, not industrial contracts with a cost
  floor; the shape is what matters. Each step is about half the previous one.
- **Label every concession and name its price.** "We can move to X if the term is 24 months." A concession that is
  not labelled is not counted as a move by a human; test whether the bots count it.
- **The last step should be small and odd-sized**, with a statement that it is the limit. It makes `final_offer` on
  their side more likely to land near us.
- **Never split the difference when they propose it.** Their offer to split concedes half; hold and ask for the rest
  in terms.

### 4.3 Trading terms (logrolling)

The fields with different value to each side, and the signal that the supplier wants the trade:

| Lever | Worth to us | Signal from the supplier |
|---|---|---|
| Payment days | Our interest rate, per case | "Faster payment is welcome" (row 5), "Faster payment would help us more than anything" (row 12), credit notes in the dossier |
| Contract length | Covers the horizon; an uncovered year costs the fallback price plus risk | "Planning security", an expiring framework contract |
| Volume commitment | Free where the forecast already covers it | "Which volume can you commit to?" (row 1, 57 times) |
| Index clause | Removes their risk premium; costs us the goal's index risk | "We can offer a Preisgleitklausel" (P08, P18), a letter blaming energy or material |
| Price effective date | Units before the date are bought at the old price | A price increase letter with a date |
| Lead time, Incoterm | € per day and freight in `C` | "With overtime we can deliver in N days", idle capacity |
| Quality terms (PPM, chargebacks) | Expected defect cost | A red scorecard, an open 8D report |

- **When price is frozen** (row 11), stop asking for price. Everything else is still open, and the score counts it.
- **Volume:** where `volume_per_year` is a field, put the forecast volume in as a commitment and ask for the price
  it earns. Where it is not, state what the forecast covers and cite it. Either beats silence.
- **Index clause:** when the supplier defends with its own index (row 2), offer the clause both ways. If the index
  justifies the rise, it must also bring the price down when it falls. The supplier has already accepted the
  standard (Shell).

### 4.4 Arguments

- **Pick by the supplier's situation, not by what we can verify.** Row 6: a verified scorecard argument rarely moves
  price. Row 2: an index we cite can support their side. Check the direction of every index before citing it.
- **Rival quotes are the strongest argument we have** (8 "took it into account", D02 and P05). This is BATNA made
  visible. Only cite real ones with IDs: an invented rival is `contradicted` and costs trust.
- **"We did not know that"** (4 times) comes from facts about the supplier's own performance or contract that the
  sales rep had not seen. Notice periods, past price paths and should-cost belong here.
- **At most two arguments per e-mail,** the strongest first.

### 4.5 Questions and tone

- **Calibrated questions** when the supplier stalls or refuses: "What would make 24 months workable for you?", "How
  can we close the gap on payment terms?". Never a question alone: row 8 shows that a message with no move counts as
  no move.
- **Label their problem first.** "We understand energy costs have hit the foundry hard this year" before the ask. It
  costs nothing and the brief says tone is read.
- **No irritators:** "fair", "generous", "reasonable" about our own offer. No threats we cannot carry out.
- **Counter the approval ladder** (rows 9 and 10): it is the "higher authority" gambit. Ask what the boss needs to
  see, give that, and ask again. Our trace shows the second ask gets the next step.
- **Counter the call stall** (row 10): restate the offer in writing with one new trade, so the round is not wasted.

### 4.6 Closing and walking

- **Compare every standing offer with the alternative in `C`.** "Some cases are best left without a deal."
- **Probe a `final_offer` once** with a trade, not with a lower price: a term that costs them nothing may still be
  open. Tactical does this when a walk-away is cheap.
- **The nibble:** before accepting, ask for one small non-price term. Check that unstated fields are not closing on
  the supplier's standard terms.
- **In RFQ cases, run the threads against each other** to the last round, and tell each supplier truthfully where it
  stands. Accept only when the leader has stopped moving.

## 5. Other options

Ways to improve beyond tuning price tactics.

1. **Model the supplier's type first, then pick the playbook.** The brief names four: the family foundry (relationship
   and memory), the group with an approval ladder (persistence, material for the boss), the job shop short of cash
   and work (payment days, volume), the near-monopolist (take terms, protect supply, consider no deal). A third of the
   final cases mix types and case types, so the mapping must come from traits in the dossier, not from supplier IDs.
2. **Estimate the floor per case** from should-cost and history, and set the anchor from it (section 4.1).
3. **Build our own supplier simulator** from the replays, as the brief suggests, to test concession curves without
   spending the 200 daily sessions.
4. **Mine the replays for what moved each supplier,** per trait, and feed that into argument selection. The trace
   gives the supplier's reasons in words.
5. **Use the LLM where judgment is needed and nowhere else:** reading the dossier, choosing the lever and the tone,
   writing the e-mail. Numbers stay in code. This is the planned `judged` strategy.
6. **Decide the no-deal cases on purpose.** Where the alternative beats the best reachable deal, spend few rounds
   and walk.

## 6. What to test

Hypotheses for benchmark runs, most promising first. Each needs at least three repetitions per case, recorded under
`agent/docs/benchmarks/`.

| # | Change | Expected effect | Basis |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Answer the volume question: commit the forecast volume where it is a field, cite the forecast where it is not | A price step in most cases | Row 1; logrolling |
| 2 | Anchor from the floor estimate instead of a fixed percentage | Higher scores on `leverage` and RFQ cases | D02 floor; Galinsky, Mussweiler |
| 3 | Offer a two-way index clause when the supplier cites its own index | Lifts P08 and P18, our lowest scores | Row 2; contingent contracts |
| 4 | Lead with payment days for suppliers flagged cash-short | Price moves where price arguments fail | Rows 5 and 12 |
| 5 | Cap arguments at two per e-mail, chosen by supplier trait | Fewer "does not change our calculation" replies | Row 6; Rackham |
| 6 | Shrinking, labelled concessions with a precise last step | A better final offer from the supplier | Ackerman; Kwon, Weingart |
| 7 | One line of appreciation and a label of their problem in each e-mail | More movement per round | Brief; Vaccaro et al. |
| 8 | A calibrated question added to every message that also contains a move | Suppliers name their lever sooner | Voss; row 8 |

The guide is written: `agent/docs/knowledge/get-best-price-guide.md` in the EHLFinal2026 repo. I put it under `agent/docs/` because that is where the other docs live; say if you want it at the repo root instead. I read "get invest price price guide" as "get best price guide".

The sources are cited from memory — I did not run a web search, so check any title, author or year before it goes on a pitch slide. Nothing was run or committed.

What's in it:

- **Ten rules**, ordered by how much I expect them to move the score.
- **Books**: twelve general ones (Getting to Yes, Negotiation Genius, Never Split the Difference, Influence, Bargaining for Advantage and others), plus procurement sources such as the Kraljic matrix. The arena's category goals map almost directly onto that matrix.
- **Research findings**: anchoring, precise offers, multiple equivalent offers, concession timing, and two studies of LLM negotiators.
- **Tactics mapped to the arena**: each one is tied to the brief's rules and to the rows in `rejections.md`.
- **Other options** beyond price tactics: supplier-type playbooks, a per-case floor estimate, our own supplier simulator, mining replays, deliberate no-deal cases.
- **Eight hypotheses to benchmark**, most promising first.

The three I would test first:

1. **Answer the volume question.** Suppliers ask "which volume can you commit to?" 57 times in our traces, and neither strategy replies.
2. **Anchor from an estimate of the supplier's floor**, not a fixed percentage below the quote. Our anchors stop at 15–18 % below, while the D02 floor was about 24 % below the opening.
3. **Offer a two-way index clause** when the supplier defends its price with its own cost index. P08 and P18 offer such a clause and are our lowest scores.

The guide rests on your assumption that the bots behave like a human sales rep. The brief supports that, with four hard-coded exceptions: the cost floor, the approval ladder, the ID check on cited data, and no concession without a move from us.

# negotiator

Buyer agent toolkit for the [Tacto Negotiation Arena](../negotiation-arena-kit/README.md): a client for every
API endpoint, a runner that plays cases (RFQ threads in parallel, Live Final waves), full telemetry, reports and
statistics, and a baseline strategy to beat.

Python 3.12 (the arena starter kit requires it); the kit is a path dependency, so the published cost function
C and the quote-PDF parsing are exactly the arena's.

## Setup

```sh
cd agent
uv sync
# the key: ARENA_API_KEY in the repo-root .env (git-ignored); ARENA_URL defaults to https://arena.tacto.ai
uv run negotiator me
```

## Commands

| Command | What |
|---|---|
| `negotiator health` / `me` | arena up, data downloads / team, practice quota, best scores |
| `negotiator cases --set practice\|sandbox\|final` · `case <id>` | case files |
| `negotiator sessions --set …` · `session <sid>` · `thread <sid> <supplier>` · `backoffice <sid>` | our sessions, state, result + trace, threads, the supplier's back office |
| `negotiator attachment <sid> <attachment_id> -o FILE` | a supplier document |
| `negotiator board` | leaderboard (for people; refused in final mode) |
| `negotiator data` | download package v1 and the Sunday release into `agent/data/` |
| `negotiator play <case_id> [--strategy tactical\|baseline]` | play one case, with telemetry and a report |
| `negotiator run --set sandbox\|practice [--cases …] [--parallel N]` | many cases in parallel (default: every hosted case of the set) |
| `negotiator final [--parallel 10]` | the Live Final: waits for each wave, plays its cases within the cap |
| `negotiator report [run_id\|latest]` · `stats` | rebuild a run's report · best/mean score per case across all runs |
| `negotiator lessons [run_id\|latest]` | per case, worst first: score, cost blocks, the supplier's reasons per round, argument checks (also written as `lessons.md` after every run) |

Global options: `--url` (e.g. a local `arena-sim`), `--key`, `--json`, `-v`.

**Quota:** practice is 200 sessions per team per rolling 24 h; sandbox (`case:D01`, `case:D02`) and `arena-sim`
are free. Develop on sandbox and the simulator, spend practice deliberately.

```sh
uv run arena-sim serve --port 8100 --data ../negotiation-arena-kit/data          # local API, scripted supplier
uv run negotiator --url http://127.0.0.1:8100 register "Team" sim                  # a simulator key
uv run negotiator --url http://127.0.0.1:8100 --key <sim key> run --set practice
```

## LLM strategy and providers

`--strategy llm` adds a model on top of the baseline: before the session opens it profiles each supplier from
its dossier (letters, notes, news, negotiation history, credit index); each round it reads the reply and picks
stance, concession, lever and arguments, and writes the e-mail text. Code still builds every term sheet from C,
inserts the checked arguments, strips IDs and figures the model wrote, and falls back to the baseline move if
the model is slow or fails.

Switch the model with one string - `--llm <provider>:<model>` or `LLM=<provider>:<model>` in `.env`:

| Spec | Protocol | Key |
|---|---|---|
| `ollama:qwen3.6:latest` (default) | OpenAI-compatible, `http://localhost:11434/v1`, thinking off | – |
| `openai:<model>` | OpenAI | `OPENAI_API_KEY` |
| `openrouter:<vendor>/<model>` | OpenAI-compatible | `OPENROUTER_API_KEY` |
| `groq:` · `mistral:` · `deepseek:` · `together:` | OpenAI-compatible | `<PROVIDER>_API_KEY` |
| `compat:<model>` | any OpenAI-compatible endpoint at `LLM_BASE_URL` | `LLM_API_KEY` |
| `anthropic:<model>` | Anthropic messages | `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY` |

Tuning: `LLM_REASONING` (`none|low|medium|high`, sent as `reasoning_effort`), `LLM_TIMEOUT_S` (default 30: each
e-mail must reach the arena within 60 s of the reply), `LLM_PARALLEL` (concurrent calls, default 4).

```sh
uv run negotiator run --set sandbox --strategy llm
uv run negotiator play case:P05 --strategy llm --llm anthropic:claude-haiku-4-5
```

## Telemetry: `runs/<run_id>/`

| File | Content |
|---|---|
| `events.jsonl` | every event: `session_opened` (opening C per supplier), `plan`, `message_sent` (sheets with C), `reply` (status, terms, C, claim results, signals, latency), `attachment`, `thread_hold`, `decision`, `conflict`, `result` |
| `http.jsonl` | every HTTP attempt: endpoint, status, latency, retry, move id, pacing wait, practice quota left |
| `run.log` | the human-readable log (debug level) |
| `sessions/<sid>.json` | the whole case: case file, e-mails both ways, documents as text, decisions with rationale, result, the arena's trace and back office |
| `sessions/<sid>/` | the documents suppliers attached (quote PDF, cost breakdown XLSX, …) |
| `metrics.json` | counters (HTTP status, claim results, supplier statuses, timeouts, deals, LLM calls, errors, tokens, fallbacks) and timings (supplier reply, decision delay after a reply, HTTP latency per endpoint, LLM latency per purpose, case duration) |
| `events.jsonl` → `llm_call`, `profile` | every model call (purpose, model, latency, tokens, output) and each supplier profile |
| `summary.json`, `report.md` | scores, C_open/C_deal/C_best/C_alt, price paths per thread, cost breakdown, claims, HTTP and timing tables |

## Architecture

```
config.py      settings from env / .env (ARENA_API_KEY, ARENA_URL, NEGOTIATOR_FINAL, …)
client.py      every endpoint; paced < 10 calls/s; safe retries with X-Move-Id; final-mode guard
telemetry.py   Recorder: events, HTTP log, metrics, transcripts, logging
data.py        data package in SQLite + facts.json; checkable Evidence (index moves, scorecard, notice, …)
profile.py     supplier traits from notes, letters, news, history (cash-short, approval ladder, hedged, …)
guards.py      hard rules before every send and accept: must-haves, alternative, valid sheets and IDs
lessons.py     lessons.md: what each case taught
session.py     Negotiation: threads, documents, costs (kit's C), send/accept/walk away, transcript
llm.py         one client for OpenAI-compatible and Anthropic APIs, switched by `provider:model`; telemetry
strategy/      Strategy protocol (prepare, decide, conclude, keepalive), baseline, llm_strategy
runner.py      play_case (one worker per thread, keepalive, deadline), play_many, play_final
report.py      summary.json, report.md, statistics across runs
cli.py         the `negotiator` command
```

A strategy only decides; `Negotiation` performs and records. To add one, implement `prepare / decide / conclude /
keepalive` (see `strategy/base.py`) and register it in `strategy/__init__.py`.

**Tactical (default):** the category goal sets the policy (anchor depth, Boulware beta, reciprocity, which
levers to trade); the supplier's profile adjusts it. Concessions are counted in C: Boulware over the rounds the
round limit and the clock leave, capped tit-for-tat by the supplier's last move (no move from it, no move from us;
a half step after two stalls; the third settles the thread). Each round sends up to three sheets of equal C: our
C-optimal terms, a trade the supplier values (early payment for the cash-short, a long commitment for those who want
volume), a pure price move. Arguments are chosen by profile; irrelevant or contradicted kinds are dropped. A final
offer is probed once only when walking would cost little. The guards (`guards.py`) refuse any accept that breaks a
must-have (read on the quote PDF's standard terms; unknown counts as broken) or loses to the alternative. The tactics
are inspired by ASTRA (Kwon et al., [DSincerity/ASTRA-NegoAgent](https://github.com/DSincerity/ASTRA-NegoAgent)):
opponent modelling, an optimiser over the cost function, offers of equal value, tit-for-tat - no code taken.

**Baseline:** a target price from the lower of opening and current price minus an anchor per category goal
(floored at should-cost, plus the sustainable margin where squeezing the supplier costs C); up to three
checkable arguments (short notice vs. contract, index moves below the asked increase, weak scorecard,
should-cost, alternative quote, a cheaper rival in an RFQ); a concession schedule; three term sheets per round
(C-optimal terms, a pure price move on the supplier's terms, a shorter-payment variant at equal C); it holds a
thread on agreed / final offer / stall / close enough / last round and accepts the cheapest standing sheet that
beats the alternative.

**Experiments** (`strategy/experiments.py`): the baseline with exactly one tactic changed each - `lowball` (a deeper
anchor), `questions` (three questions per e-mail), `polite` / `shelby` (tone), `budget` (a ceiling "set by
management" that we do not cross), `trade` (no move without a move, said so). They exist to measure a tactic, not to
win; the runs are in [`docs/benchmarks/`](docs/benchmarks/).

## Tests

uv run pytest        # unit tests + end to end against a local arena-sim (started by the tests)
uv run ruff check . && uv run ruff format --check .

"""Single-tactic experiments on top of the baseline: each variant changes one thing, so a benchmark run
shows what that tactic alone is worth against the supplier bots (results: docs/benchmarks/).

  lowball    a deeper opening anchor: ask for less than we need, so the middle lands in our favour
  questions  three questions in every e-mail: make answering us more work than agreeing
  polite     a warm, appreciative tone
  shelby     a curt, hard tone with a threat to place the order elsewhere
  budget     a ceiling set by a third party ("management released at most EUR X") that we do not cross
  trade      no price move without a move from the supplier, and said so: every option is a trade

Everything else - term sheets from C, arguments, holding and closing - is the baseline's.
"""

from dataclasses import dataclass

from negotiator.session import Negotiation
from negotiator.strategy.baseline import GOAL_ANCHOR, BaselineStrategy, SupplierPlan
from negotiator.telemetry import log

# tone -> (first e-mail, later e-mails, closing line or None)
TONES = {
    "polite": (
        "thank you very much for your quote and for the good cooperation - we appreciate the work your team puts "
        "into it. We would like to find a solution that works for both sides; as it stands the quote is above what "
        "we can accept.",
        "thank you for your reply and for moving towards us - we appreciate it. We have moved as well and hope you "
        "can take a further step.",
        "Thank you for your support - we are confident we will find an agreement.",
    ),
    "shelby": (
        "we have read your quote. It is not a number we will sign.",
        "you have moved a little. It is not enough. We have moved too, and we do not move twice for nothing.",
        "This order will be placed either way - with you or without you. Your move.",
    ),
}
QUESTIONS = [
    "What lead time can you commit to for the first call-off?",
    "Which share of your price is material, and which index does it follow?",
    "How much free capacity do you have for this part in the coming quarter?",
    "Who on your side has to approve a price below your quote?",
    "Would faster payment or a longer commitment help you more?",
    "What defect rate do you achieve on comparable parts?",
    "What would a higher annual volume change in your calculation?",
    "Which Incoterm and packaging are cheapest for you?",
    "Can you hold the price for the whole term without an index clause?",
]


@dataclass(frozen=True)
class Tactic:
    name: str
    anchor_scale: float = 1.0  # multiplies the baseline's anchor per category goal
    tone: str | None = None  # a key of TONES; None: the baseline's wording
    questions_per_round: int = 0
    budget_share: float | None = None  # ceiling = target + share x (opening - target); None: no ceiling
    conditional: bool = False  # the supplier does not move -> we do not move at all


TACTICS = {
    t.name: t
    for t in (
        Tactic("lowball", anchor_scale=1.5),
        Tactic("questions", questions_per_round=3),
        Tactic("polite", tone="polite"),
        Tactic("shelby", tone="shelby"),
        Tactic("budget", budget_share=0.5),
        Tactic("trade", conditional=True),
    )
}


class ExperimentStrategy(BaselineStrategy):
    def __init__(self, tactic: Tactic, data=None, llm=None) -> None:
        super().__init__(data, llm)
        self.tactic = tactic
        self.name = tactic.name
        self.ceilings: dict[str, float] = {}

    def prepare(self, neg: Negotiation) -> None:
        super().prepare(neg)
        tac = self.tactic
        goal = neg.buyer.get("category_goal", "leverage")
        current = neg.buyer.get("current_unit_price")
        for sid, plan in self.plans.items():
            if plan.open_price is None or plan.target_price is None:
                continue
            if tac.anchor_scale != 1.0:
                base = min(plan.open_price, current) if current else plan.open_price
                target = base * (1 - GOAL_ANCHOR.get(goal, 0.06) * tac.anchor_scale)
                plan.target_price = round(min(max(target, plan.floor_price or 0.0), plan.open_price), 2)
            if tac.budget_share is not None:
                gap = plan.open_price - plan.target_price
                self.ceilings[sid] = round(plan.target_price + tac.budget_share * gap, 2)
            neg.recorder.event(
                "experiment",
                session_id=neg.session_id,
                case_id=neg.case_id,
                supplier_id=sid,
                tactic=tac.name,
                target_price=plan.target_price,
                ceiling=self.ceilings.get(sid),
            )
            log.info("%s %s: target %s ceiling %s", sid, tac.name, plan.target_price, self.ceilings.get(sid))

    def _next_price(self, plan: SupplierPlan, theirs, ours, round_index, their_path=None) -> float:
        price = super()._next_price(plan, theirs, ours, round_index, their_path)
        if self.tactic.conditional and ours and their_path and len(their_path) >= 2:
            if their_path[-1] >= their_path[-2]:
                price = ours[-1]
        ceiling = self.ceilings.get(plan.supplier_id)
        if ceiling is not None:
            price = min(price, max(ceiling, ours[-1] if ours else 0.0))
        return price

    def _opener(self, first: bool) -> str:
        if self.tactic.tone is None:
            return super()._opener(first)
        return TONES[self.tactic.tone][0 if first else 1]

    def _extra_lines(self, neg: Negotiation, plan: SupplierPlan, first: bool) -> list[str]:
        tac, lines = self.tactic, []
        ceiling = self.ceilings.get(plan.supplier_id)
        if ceiling is not None:
            lines.append(
                f"Our management has released a fixed budget for this part: EUR {ceiling:,.2f} per unit on the terms "
                "of option A is the most I am allowed to sign."
                if first
                else f"The budget ceiling of EUR {ceiling:,.2f} per unit on the terms of option A stands; I cannot "
                "sign above it."
            )
        if tac.conditional:
            lines.append(
                "We do not pay more without something in return: each option below gives you something you can use "
                "(commitment, payment or delivery terms) at the price it asks. If you need a higher price, tell us "
                "which term you give for it."
            )
        if tac.questions_per_round:
            start = neg.threads[plan.supplier_id].rounds_used * tac.questions_per_round
            lines += [QUESTIONS[(start + i) % len(QUESTIONS)] for i in range(tac.questions_per_round)]
        if tac.tone and TONES[tac.tone][2]:
            lines.append(TONES[tac.tone][2])
        return lines

from negotiator.strategy.baseline import BaselineStrategy

from negotiator.strategy.llm_strategy import LLMStrategy
from negotiator.strategy.tactical import TacticalStrategy

STRATEGIES: dict[str, Callable[..., Strategy]] = {
    "tactical": TacticalStrategy,
    "baseline": BaselineStrategy,
    "llm": LLMStrategy,
    **{name: partial(ExperimentStrategy, tactic) for name, tactic in TACTICS.items()},
}
NEEDS_LLM = {"llm"}

"""The strategy interface. The runner calls it; `Negotiation` holds the state it reads.

Per thread the runner asks `decide(neg, supplier_id)`:
  message    send this e-mail (subject, body, term sheets, refs)
  hold       this thread is settled for now (agreed, final offer, close enough, out of rounds)
  drop       this thread is over for us (walked away, no bid, hopeless)
  accept     close the case on this supplier's standing term sheet
  walk_away  close the case without a deal
When every thread is held or dropped, `conclude(neg)` makes the closing move (accept or walk away).
While other threads still negotiate, a held thread's 60 s clock keeps running: `keepalive` returns a
message that keeps it alive (or None to let it be).
"""

from dataclasses import dataclass, field
from typing import Literal, Protocol

from negotiator.session import Negotiation

Kind = Literal["message", "hold", "drop", "accept", "walk_away"]


@dataclass
class Decision:
    kind: Kind
    supplier_id: str | None = None
    message: dict | None = None
    term_sheet_id: str | None = None
    rationale: dict = field(default_factory=dict)

    @classmethod
    def hold(cls, supplier_id: str, why: str, **extra) -> "Decision":
        return cls("hold", supplier_id, rationale={"why": why, **extra})

    @classmethod
    def drop(cls, supplier_id: str, why: str, **extra) -> "Decision":
        return cls("drop", supplier_id, rationale={"why": why, **extra})

    def conclude(self, neg: Negotiation) -> Decision: ...

    def keepalive(self, neg: Negotiation, supplier_id: str) -> dict | None: ...

"""The simulated supplier: one value V per round, moved by what the buyer just did.

Nothing here is a rule of the arena - the arena does not hand out its suppliers. It is the smallest model that
reproduces what the recorded sessions show:

  - the supplier answers on the buyer's sheet it likes best, at its own price for that structure;
  - it concedes a share of the gap between its price and its floor, and how large a share depends on what
    the buyer did: moved, stood still, brought a rival quote or another argument that convinced it;
  - a big step comes in two halves ("we need to clarify this internally"), the second on the next e-mail;
  - after a few rounds it calls its offer final and mostly stays there;
  - it agrees as soon as a sheet the buyer sent is worth its new price.

Step shares and the round of the final offer are not parameters but resampled from the recorded moves of that
supplier (pooled over all suppliers where it has too few), so the simulator is as noisy as the bots are.
"""

@dataclass
class ThreadState:
    supplier_id: str
    messages: list[dict] = field(default_factory=list)  # both directions, in order; ours: from=buyer
    last_reply_at: float = field(default_factory=time.monotonic)
    timeouts: int = 0
    closed: str | None = None
    lock: threading.Lock = field(default_factory=threading.Lock, repr=False)

    @property
    def supplier_messages(self) -> list[dict]:
        return [m for m in self.messages if m.get("from") != "buyer"]

    @property
    def latest(self) -> dict:
        msgs = self.supplier_messages
        return msgs[-1] if msgs else {}

    @property
    def status(self) -> str:
        return "closed" if self.closed else self.latest.get("status", "open")

    @property
    def live(self) -> bool:
        return not self.closed and self.status not in ENDED_STATUSES

    @property
    def standing(self) -> tuple[str | None, dict]:
        sheets = self.latest.get("term_sheets") or []
        return (sheets[0]["term_sheet_id"], sheets[0]["terms"]) if sheets else (None, {})

    @property
    def rounds_used(self) -> int:
        return sum(1 for m in self.messages if m.get("from") == "buyer" and not m.get("action"))

    @property
    def standard_terms(self) -> dict:
        """The supplier's standard terms from its latest quote PDF: what closes for a missing field."""
        for msg in reversed(self.supplier_messages):
            for att in msg.get("attachments") or []:
                if att.get("name", "").startswith("quote") and att.get("text"):
                    return quote_terms(att["text"]).get("standard", {})
        return {}

    def price_path(self) -> list[float]:
        out = []
        for m in self.supplier_messages:
            sheets = m.get("term_sheets") or []
            if sheets and sheets[0]["terms"].get("unit_price") is not None:
                out.append(sheets[0]["terms"]["unit_price"])
        return out

    def our_price_path(self) -> list[float]:
        return [
            m["term_sheets"][0]["terms"]["unit_price"]
            for m in self.messages
            if m.get("from") == "buyer"
            and m.get("term_sheets")
            and m["term_sheets"][0]["terms"].get("unit_price") is not None
        ]

    def seconds_since_reply(self) -> float:
        return time.monotonic() - self.last_reply_at

result.output:
## What counts

**Term sheets bind** - nothing else. They are taken exactly as you send them, never guessed from
prose; the deal is the term sheet you accept.

**Data you cite is checked.** Cite the data by ID (in the body or in `refs`) and write your figure
in the same sentence; the arena checks it against the data package (`facts.json`) and reports each
check in the reply's `claim_results` - at most 3 per message, so write one argument per sentence.
Order lines of different parts are separate arguments, so citing orders for three parts uses all
three. Without a figure, the data's own value is taken. IDs of meeting notes, suppliers or parts
are context, not checks.

| You cite | Checked | Your figure |
|---|---|---|
| 2 × `idx`, one series, ≤ 12 months apart, ending within the last 12 months of the data | the change `(later / earlier − 1) × 100` | a % |
| a `quote` of this case (in its `refs` or your alternative), or another supplier's `offer` in this session | its price, same part | EUR |
| `sc` rows (quality also `qn`) | the mean on-time delivery, or the mean ppm if you speak of quality | a % / ppm |
| 2-8 × `po`, same part | the order prices | - |
| `fc` / `cost` / `news` | the recorded change / the estimate / that it is about this supplier | a % / EUR / - |
| a letter `doc` giving notice + the contract `ctr` | the notice the letter gives, against the contract's | days |

Tolerance: ±0.5 percentage points for %, else ±0.5 % (at least 0.01). Results: `verified` - the
data matches; whether and how far it moves the supplier is the supplier's business. `irrelevant` -
true, but not about this supplier or part, or an index window too long or too old.
`contradicted` - an unknown ID or a wrong figure: it costs trust. `duplicate` - each ID counts
once per case, except a rival's quote: in an RFQ you may cite it to every other bidder, and it
counts once per supplier. Citing a buyer-private fact - a rival quote - reveals it to the
supplier you cite it to.

**Verified is not the same as convincing.** A supplier's hard limits come from its own economics
    def fact(self, ref: str) -> dict | None:
        return self.facts.get(ref)

    def with_case(self, case: dict) -> "WorldData":
        """Case-only facts (hidden cases) become citable for this case."""
        if case.get("facts"):
            self.facts = {**self.facts, **case["facts"]}
        return self

    def document_text(self, doc_id: str) -> str | None:
        rows = self.query("SELECT file FROM documents WHERE id = ?", (doc_id,))
        for base in [self.root] + ([self.release] if self.release else []):
            if rows and rows[0]["file"] and (base / rows[0]["file"]).is_file():
                return (base / rows[0]["file"]).read_text(encoding="utf-8")
        return None

    # ------------------------------------------------------------------ dossier
    def evidence_should_cost(self, part_ids: list[str], price: float) -> list[Evidence]:
        out = []
        for row in self.query(
            f"SELECT id, unit_cost FROM should_cost WHERE part_id IN ({','.join('?' for _ in part_ids)})",
            tuple(part_ids),
        ):
            if row["unit_cost"] and price > row["unit_cost"] * 1.12:
                out.append(
                    Evidence(
                        kind="should_cost",
                        refs=[row["id"]],
                        sentence=f"Our should-cost estimate for this part is EUR {row['unit_cost']:.2f} ({row['id']}).",
                        strength=(price / row["unit_cost"] - 1) * 5,
                        meta={"unit_cost": row["unit_cost"]},
                    )
                )
        return out

    def evidence_quote(self, quote_id: str | None) -> list[Evidence]:
        """The buyer's alternative quote, if the case has one."""
        q = self.fact(quote_id) if quote_id else None
        if not q or q.get("unit_price") is None:
            return []
        return [
            Evidence(
                kind="quote",
                refs=[quote_id],
                sentence=f"We hold another quote at EUR {q['unit_price']:.2f} ({quote_id}).",
                strength=1.0,
                meta={"unit_price": q["unit_price"]},
            )
        ]
